flashcards.q: What's the honest, complete answer to 'does TDD work,' with numbers?
flashcards.a: Cited industrial studies (IBM, Microsoft) report 40-90% defect-density reductions for TDD-developed code, but the same research finds real short-term productivity costs, especially for engineers new to the discipline. Benefit is strongest for complex/long-lived logic, weakest for exploratory/actively-changing design.

flashcards.q: What's the 2026-specific argument for TDD that has nothing to do with defect rates?
flashcards.a: A failing test written first is often the only falsifiable oracle an AI coding agent can build against -- a vague prompt lets the agent confidently build on a wrong assumption, while a test that must pass pins down what 'correct' means before implementation starts.

flashcards.q: What common mechanism determines whether a testing-practice adoption effort (TDD, contract testing, Testcontainers, chaos) survives past six months?
flashcards.a: Whether the cost of SKIPPING the practice is made visible and immediate (a CI gate, a deploy block, a tracked ticket with a deadline) rather than deferred to a future incident. Individual discipline with no enforcement erodes under deadline pressure; a gate survives because it isn't a request.

flashcards.q: Why does a team's actual pyramid/trophy test-shape ratio often not reflect a deliberate choice?
flashcards.a: The ratio is a lagging indicator of what's CONVENIENT to write -- a mock requires no shared infra, a real-dependency integration test does. The fix is making the correctly-shaped test as convenient as the mock (e.g. a one-line Testcontainers fixture), not just documenting that it's better.

flashcards.q: Why does contract testing adoption fail more often for organizational reasons than technical ones?
flashcards.a: It requires a PROVIDER team to do ongoing verification work whose payoff accrues to a different CONSUMER team's on-call rotation -- an incentive mismatch, not a tooling gap. Rollouts that survive start with the highest-incident-cost boundary so the provider's own recent pain motivates the investment.

flashcards.q: Why do Testcontainers rollouts commonly revert to mocks within a quarter?
flashcards.a: An ownership gap, not a technical flaw -- a flaky container startup (port collision, image pull timeout) with no assigned owner gets blamed on 'the tests,' and after enough unresolved flakiness the team reverts to mocks, which never flake that way even though they miss real bugs.

flashcards.q: Why does chaos engineering have the steepest adoption curve of the four practices in this module?
flashcards.a: Its prerequisite -- mature observability and a fast, tested rollback mechanism -- has to exist BEFORE the practice is safe to run at all, not as a refinement added later. Skipping it risks the first ambitious experiment becoming a real incident, killing appetite for the whole practice.

flashcards.q: A green, 100%-coverage AI-generated test suite still let a regression ship. What's the diagnosis?
flashcards.a: Tests asserting mock-call structure or implementation details rather than observable behavior -- coverage measures execution, not verification. No assertion would fail if the actual bug were introduced. Fix: periodic mutation testing (mutmut/Stryker/PIT) to measure whether tests would catch a deliberately broken implementation.

flashcards.q: Why is adopting all four testing practices (TDD, contract testing, Testcontainers, chaos) simultaneously as one 'quality initiative' usually a mistake?
flashcards.a: Each has a distinct adoption obstacle requiring dedicated organizational attention; attempting all four at once dilutes the focus any single one needs to actually stick. Better: sequence by matching the practice to the org's actual recent incident root cause.

flashcards.q: A CI gate enforces 'new logic requires a new test,' but a mutation-testing audit shows most tests would still pass against broken implementations. What does this reveal about gate-based enforcement?
flashcards.a: A presence-based gate enforces the mechanical FORM of a practice (a test file exists) but not its QUALITY. This isn't a failure of the practice -- it's the expected limit of presence gates, requiring a second, quality-measuring layer (mutation score thresholds) on top.

flashcards.q: When is TDD's case weakest, and why does mandating it there add pure overhead?
flashcards.a: For exploratory or actively-changing design work (early prototyping, UI layout likely to be discarded) -- writing a precise test against a design about to be thrown away has no corresponding payoff.
